days.label: Day 01
days.title: The foundation
days.subtitle: Laptop, ROS 2 Jazzy & a fresh SD card
days.intro: You reported installing ROS 2 Jazzy on your laptop and preparing a Raspberry Pi SD card on Day 1. Your confirmed hardware is a Raspberry Pi 4B, a TurtleBot Burger, and a 32 GB SanDisk microSD card. Later terminal evidence confirms that the Pi currently runs Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (Noble Numbat), arm64. The exact original image filename and flashing sequence have not been supplied. Detailed installation commands below are reference instructions, not recovered terminal history.

steps.title: Check the operating system
steps.body: Reference procedure, not a recovered terminal history. These apt instructions assume Ubuntu 24.04 (Noble). Do not apply them unchanged to Raspberry Pi OS or Ubuntu 22.04.

commands.why: Prints the Linux distribution and version. Look for Ubuntu and VERSION_ID="24.04".
Prints the package architecture: typically amd64 on a laptop or arm64 on a 64-bit Pi installation.

steps.check: Record the actual OS and architecture before continuing.

steps.title: Prepare a UTF-8 locale
steps.body: A locale defines language and text encoding. An existing UTF-8 locale is fine; the following is an example configuration.

commands.why: Shows the current language and encoding settings.

commands.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install locales
commands.why: Refreshes the package index, then installs locale management tools. sudo runs with administrator privileges.

commands.code:
sudo locale-gen en_US en_US.UTF-8
sudo update-locale LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 LANG=en_US.UTF-8
export LANG=en_US.UTF-8
commands.why: Generates locale data, saves defaults, and sets the language in this shell.

steps.check: Run locale again and check for UTF-8.

steps.title: Connect Ubuntu to the ROS package repository
steps.body: Ubuntu needs the ROS package source before apt can find Jazzy. This uses the official ros2-apt-source package. Run each block in the same terminal and stop if a download fails.

commands.code:
sudo apt install software-properties-common curl
sudo add-apt-repository universe
commands.why: Installs repository tools and curl, then enables Ubuntu’s Universe software collection.

Refreshes apt. The pipeline fetches the latest release metadata, selects tag_name, and extracts its value. $(...) captures output; export makes the variable available to child processes. Check that a version was printed.
Downloads the package for this Ubuntu codename. -f fails on HTTP errors, -L follows redirects, and -o selects the output file. dpkg installs the repository configuration package.

steps.check: The download and dpkg command must both succeed.

steps.title: Install Jazzy on the laptop
steps.body: Use the desktop package for a development laptop. Review proposed upgrades before accepting them.

commands.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop
commands.why: Refreshes packages, upgrades installed software, and installs Jazzy with desktop tools.
Loads ROS into the current Bash terminal, then prints the selected ROS distribution.
Optional: adds the setup line to future interactive Bash sessions only if absent. || runs the second command when the first does not find a match. >> appends.

steps.check: ROS_DISTRO should print jazzy. This is an expected result, not an observed result from your laptop.

steps.title: Test two ROS nodes
steps.body: Open two terminals. A node is a running ROS program; a topic carries typed messages between nodes.

commands.why: Terminal A: ros2 run starts the talker executable from the demo_nodes_cpp package.
Terminal B: starts the Python listener. Keep the talker running.

steps.check: The listener should receive the talker’s messages. Stop each with Ctrl+C; record your actual output.

steps.title: Write the Raspberry Pi SD card
steps.body:
You install an operating-system image onto the SD card; the Raspberry Pi is the computer that boots it. Your card is a 32 GB SanDisk, used with a Raspberry Pi 4B and TurtleBot Burger. Your terminal output confirms Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (Noble Numbat), arm64, on the Pi. This identifies the currently running OS; it does not establish the original image filename, original point release, or whether the image was Server or Desktop. The following flashing sequence is a reference reconstruction. For this Ubuntu/Jazzy reference path, choose a compatible Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS 64-bit image for your exact Pi model.

1. Install and open Raspberry Pi Imager from the official Raspberry Pi website.
2. Select your exact Pi model and the intended OS image (or use a downloaded compatible image).
3. Select the microSD card by capacity/device name. Writing erases the selected device; check it carefully.
4. If that image supports customisation, set hostname, username, networking, and SSH; otherwise finish setup with a keyboard and display after boot. Do not publish passwords or SSH private keys.
5. Write, wait for verification, safely eject, insert into the powered-off Pi, then connect a suitable power supply.
6. Allow the first boot to finish. Record the image filename, Pi model, and first successful login.
steps.check: Verified from your supplied terminal output: the Pi runs Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, codename noble, architecture arm64. The original image filename and exact flashing procedure remain to be recorded; no reflash is needed to identify the current OS.

The OS check below is observed evidence; the remaining setup and communication steps are reference instructions. Jazzy is the ROS release, not the operating system.

steps.title: Log in and verify the Pi operating system
steps.body: You supplied terminal output from the Pi confirming its operating system and architecture. This evidence was provided later while documenting the build; its execution on Day 2 is not established. If connecting remotely, use your configured username and address in place of PI_USER and PI_IP. The SSH command is a reference example, not a recovered command.

commands.why: Opens an encrypted terminal on the Pi. On first connection, verify the host fingerprint using a trusted local view of the Pi.
Confirms which machine you are on, its OS version, and its package architecture.

steps.check: Observed: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, Noble, arm64 (64-bit ARM). This confirms the Pi OS and architecture only; it does not prove ROS is installed or that laptop–Pi communication works.

steps.title: Install ROS on the Pi
steps.body: Repeat Day 1’s UTF-8 locale and ROS repository steps on the Pi itself. Installing ROS on the laptop does not install it on the Pi.

commands.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros-base ros-jazzy-demo-nodes-cpp
commands.why: Installs the smaller ROS base and the demonstration executables used in the communication check.
Loads Jazzy into this terminal and checks the selected distribution.

steps.check: Expected: jazzy. Record any package error before moving on.

steps.title: Put both machines in the same ROS domain
steps.body: Use the same local network, avoiding guest/client isolation. The domain number is an example; use the same number on both devices. This shell configuration must be repeated in each ROS terminal. This reference assumes DDS middleware; these discovery variables do not configure rmw_zenoh.

commands.why: Loads ROS, chooses a shared discovery domain, and allows discovery on the local subnet. These exports affect this shell and its child processes.

steps.check: Matching domain IDs alone do not guarantee discovery: network, firewall, and middleware settings also matter.

steps.title: Prove laptop ↔ Pi messaging
steps.body: This is a suggested verification, not a confirmed Day 2 result.

commands.why: On the Pi, starts a publisher. Leave it running.
On the laptop, starts the listener after the environment block above.

commands.code:
ros2 topic list
ros2 node list
commands.why: In another configured terminal, lists discovered topics and nodes.

steps.check: Look for received messages on the laptop. Save a short output sample, then stop the demos with Ctrl+C.

ROS installation is only the foundation. You confirmed TurtleBot Burger and Raspberry Pi 4B. days.label: Git & GitHub
days.title: Give the journey a home
days.subtitle: Your supplied commands, explained line by line
days.status: Commands supplied by you · execution not evidenced
days.intro: These are the initial repository commands you pasted. They belong in a project folder on your development computer, not in an arbitrary system directory. Keep this setup chapter separate from your day numbering until you decide when it happened.

steps.title: Create the first commit
steps.body: These bootstrap commands are for a new repository. Do not repeat them as your daily update routine.

commands.why: echo prints the Markdown title. >> appends it to README.md, creating the file if needed. Repeating this adds duplicate titles.
Creates local Git metadata so this folder can track file revisions.
Stages only README.md for the next commit. Other files are not included.
Records the staged snapshot with a message. Git needs your configured author name and email.
Renames the current branch to main. -M permits replacing an existing branch name; use carefully in an established repository.
Registers this GitHub URL as the remote named origin. It does not create the GitHub repository.
Uploads main and remembers origin/main as its upstream. Requires repository access and working GitHub authentication.

steps.check: Expected: the committed README appears on GitHub.

steps.title: Publish later journal updates
steps.body: Use this routine after editing docs/journal.json. The build regenerates both the readable Markdown document and the interactive website from the same content.

commands.why: Regenerates JOURNAL.md and docs/index.html. No third-party Python packages are needed.

commands.code:
git add docs/journal.json docs/index.html docs/JOURNAL.md JOURNAL.md
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Document the next TurtleBot day"
git push
commands.why: Stages the journal changes, lets you review them, saves a commit, and uploads it. The Pages workflow publishes the docs folder.

steps.check: Check the Pages workflow in the repository’s Actions tab.
